questions.worked_solution:
We recall the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{5})}^{x}.$

First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{5}{2}\cdot {7}^{-x}) & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{({7}^{-1})}^{x} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013814/assets/f2858b7d6adc07c0f2196bbe8170f17fa02aff19d494726c08f7c03a419afd53.png)

From the graph, we see that the function approaches zero as $x$ increases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{5}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}=\frac{5}{2}\cdot 0=0.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Infinite Limits Using the Laws of Exponents and the Algebra of Limits
questions.worked_solution:
We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }-2\cdot {e}^{4x-3} & =-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{4x-3} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }({e}^{-3}\cdot {e}^{4x}) \\  & =-2\cdot {e}^{-3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{4x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{{e}^{3}}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }({e}^{4})^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={({e}^{4})}^{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013814/assets/6590b80777c49b3d018fa38ce79c7fb14103365f783dac18135b8d3637ee724d.png)

From the graph, we see that the function increases without bound as $x$ increases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }({e}^{4})^{x}=\infty .
$$

The negative factor $-\frac{2}{{e}^{3}}$ changes the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

$$
-\frac{2}{{e}^{3}}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }({e}^{4})^{x}=-\frac{2}{{e}^{3}}\cdot \infty =-\infty .
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Infinite Limits Using the Laws of Exponents and the Algebra of Limits
questions.worked_solution:
We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{5}^{3-2x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({5}^{3}\cdot {5}^{-2x}) \\  & ={5}^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{5}^{-2x} \\  & =125\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{({5}^{-2})}^{x} \\  & =125\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{{5}^{2}})}^{x} \\  & =125\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{25})}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{25})}^{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013814/assets/3795890dac6f542c8aa75d61deb8a03192a41532270b74eafcd972e82ac6721e.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ increases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{25})}^{x}=0.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{5}^{3-2x}=125\cdot 0=0.
$$
